column2: dingTalkChannel implements a DingTalk custom bot.
Platform constraints that shape this implementation:
- Each bot is limited to 20 messages/minute; excess messages may be silently dropped (even with HTTP 200),
so rate limiting must be client-side; see DefaultRatePerMin.
- Security supports signing, custom keywords, or an IP allowlist. Signing is the only option independent of
message content, so only signing is supported (as are bare webhooks with all three options disabled).
- Both success and failure return HTTP 200; inspect errcode in the body, or failed deliveries
will be recorded as successful.
The DingTalk Webhook URL contains access_token and is itself a credential; mask it entirely.
The destination is the DingTalk Webhook URL itself; changing it requires explicitly resupplying the signing key for the new URL.
Send delivers one message. Use ActionCard with a button for a single item with a backlink; otherwise use markdown.
DingTalk markdown has no explicit byte limit, but cap it defensively against oversized evidence fields.
DingTalk embeds business errors in HTTP 200 responses.
301000 means signature verification failed; 310000 means keyword mismatch. Both are configuration errors
that retries cannot repair.
dingTalkSignedURL appends timestamp and sign to the webhook using the official signing rules.
Rule: string to sign = timestamp + "\n" + secret; the HMAC-SHA256 **key is also secret**.
Base64-encode the result, then URL-encode it. timestamp is in milliseconds. Return unchanged when secret is empty,
to support bots without signing enabled.
Do not pass err through: url.Parse error text includes the full URL, including access_token.
validateHTTPURL checks URL validity and supported schemes, and checks literal IP destinations for internal addresses.
Two important details:
1. **Errors must be redacted.** url.Parse returns *url.Error, whose Error() includes
**the complete original URL**. These providers embed credentials in URLs (DingTalk access_token,
WeCom key, Telegram bot token, Feishu hook id). Previously a direct `return err`
leaked credentials through the invalid-URL error into the test endpoint's 400 response,
delivery last_error records, server logs, and delivery-history responses.
2. **Check literal IPs immediately**; defer domain checks to dialing (blockInternalDial is the final
enforcement point and also handles DNS rebinding). This early check provides feedback when saving configuration,
rather than waiting for the first failed delivery.
Scheme restrictions are defensive: file:///gopher:// and similar schemes can produce unexpected http.Client
behavior (already blocked by the scheme check, with no reason to expose this surface).
emailDialTimeout / emailSessionTimeout bound connection establishment and the entire SMTP session, respectively.
net/smtp has no timeout mechanism. Without these two bounds, a stalled peer can leave
the delivery goroutine blocked forever. Since the dispatcher processes serially in one goroutine,
that would stop the entire notification system.
emailChannel implements SMTP email delivery.
Email has no platform rate limit, but should not spam recipients; use a generous default.
Mask only the password. SMTP host, account, and recipients are not secrets; masking them only complicates editing.
host/port determine which server receives the password; tls determines transport encryption. Changing any of these
requires explicitly resupplying the password, so disabling TLS also requires explicit credentials rather than an incidental edit.
STARTTLS: upgrade when supported. Never send credentials in a plaintext session (see auth below).
smtp.PlainAuth refuses to send credentials over an unencrypted connection unless the destination is localhost.
This is **correct** security behavior and must not be bypassed, but explain the cause clearly;
otherwise users see only "unencrypted connection" without knowing how to fix it.
A failed Quit does not change the fact that the server accepted the message; ignore that error.
Email is not truncated (the entire HTML body is sent); count the whole batch as delivered.
emailDial establishes an SMTP connection.
implicitTLS=true uses immediate TLS, as on port 465; false connects in plaintext on 25/587 and then uses
STARTTLS. Do not mix them: a plaintext greeting to port 465 causes an immediate disconnect.
Set the session deadline **at connection establishment**, not afterward: net/smtp.Client hides the underlying
connection in an unexported field. Once handed over, the previously set deadline is the only
fallback. It also covers blocking during the handshake.
Control attaches blockInternalDial, sharing the HTTP channels' guard. Without it SMTP
would leave an SSRF gap: host values such as 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1 could connect directly,
and smtp.NewClient handshake failures include the peer's response line in errors, which last_error
exposes through delivery history, creating a semi-blind read primitive. Timing differences between refusal and timeout
could also probe ports. Dial-time enforcement is final and also covers DNS rebinding.
smtpStageError classifies a stage failure as retryable or permanent using the SMTP reply code.
The distinction matters because SMTP 4xx and 5xx have entirely different semantics:
- 4xx (450 greylisting, 451 local error, 452 insufficient storage) are **temporary** refusals;
retry later. Greylisting in particular occurs on nearly every first delivery attempt.
- 5xx (550 unknown user, 553 invalid address) are permanent refusals; retrying is pointless.
Classifying all failures as permanent would move **every** notification to failed on its first
attempt against a greylisting server, precisely where automatic retries are most useful.
Read the first three digits of the error text as the reply code; if unavailable, treat it as retryable
(prefer an extra retry over permanently rejecting a potentially transient failure because parsing failed).
smtpReplyCode extracts the leading three-digit reply code from SMTP error text, or returns 0 if absent.
net/smtp exposes no error-code field, so parse text in the form "450 4.7.1 ...".
buildEmailMessage assembles a complete RFC 5322 message.
Base64-encode the body for two reasons: SMTP limits lines to 1000 bytes, while HTML
bodies (especially batch emails) easily exceed that; base64 also never produces lines starting with ".",
avoiding SMTP dot-stuffing concerns.
Chinese subjects require RFC 2047 encoding, or clients display garbled text.
Email has no hard length limit, so do not truncate the body.
Wrap base64 at 76 characters per line, per RFC 2045.
feishuChannel implements Feishu (including Lark) custom bots using interactive cards.
Platform characteristics:
- The signing algorithm **differs** from DingTalk and is easy to get wrong; see feishuSign.
- Like DingTalk, business errors appear in HTTP 200 bodies (code != 0).
- Card headers support color templates; map severity to colors for quick recognition in message lists.
Feishu custom bots allow approximately 5 requests/second, equivalent to 100 requests/minute.
The last Webhook URL segment uniquely identifies the bot and is a credential.
Likewise, changing the Webhook URL requires explicitly resupplying the signing key for the new URL.
Signing parameters are at the same level as the message and appear only when secret is configured.
Some Feishu hook versions use these field names; support them too.
feishuSign computes a signature according to the official Feishu rules.
This is particularly easy to get wrong; the official example is:
That means **key = timestamp + "\n" + secret, with an empty message**, not the intuitive
key=secret, message=stringToSign, which is DingTalk's algorithm. The two algorithms reverse these roles;
copying the other provider's implementation necessarily fails signature verification (19021).
feishuSeverityTemplate maps vulnerability severity to card header color templates.
Use grey for unknown severity, not blue, to avoid confusion with low.
feishuMaxCardBytes is a conservative card-content limit. Feishu rejects an entire oversized card;
choose a value well below the official limit to allow for JSON wrapper overhead.
feishuCard builds an interactive card and returns it with **the number of items actually included**.
kept serves the same purpose as in markdownBody: only items actually included should be marked delivered.
Pack whole items before constructing the header: the header describes the remaining N items continuing in the next message,
so N must come from the number actually fitted.
feishuItemLines renders the lark_md body of a single vulnerability.
Like markdown, lark_md parses links and emphasis, so all externally sourced
fields pass through markdownText (single-line conversion and escaping); otherwise a vulnerability title
could become a clickable external link in Feishu.
feishuBatchLine renders one entry in a batch card.
Filter is the contract for notification_channels.filter, a JSONB column containing channel-instance filters.
All fields are optional; omitted means no filtering, also the fallback for malformed configuration; see ParseFilter.
MinSeverity is the minimum severity threshold (low/medium/high/critical); empty means no threshold.
Empty TaskIDs / AssetIDs arrays mean unrestricted; otherwise the event must intersect them.
Empty VulnClassInclude accepts all; otherwise vulnclass must match at least one keyword.
VulnClassExclude rejects any keyword match (exclusion takes precedence over inclusion).
Matching uses case-insensitive substrings, safer than regex: invalid user regex cannot silently disable the channel.
OnStatusChange controls whether the channel receives vulnerability status-change events (meaningful only in realtime mode).
ParseFilter parses channel filter configuration.
**Never returns an error.** This is deliberate: malformed filter configuration falls back to a zero-value
Filter (= no filtering = match all), because in a vulnerability notification system **an extra notification is better than
silently missing a critical one**. Treating parse failure as no delivery gives users a channel that looks configured
but sends nothing, the worst failure mode.
On parse failure, f remains zero-valued, meaning no filtering.
ValidMinSeverity reports whether s is a valid severity threshold (empty means no threshold).
Validate checks fields with **restricted values** when saving a channel.
Why reject at write time: Match evaluates unknown thresholds as `rank >= 0`, always true;
thus a typo in min_severity ("hgih") **silently disables filtering** and
pushes everything. This aligns with the package's preference for extra delivery over missed delivery,
but users believe severity filtering is active while every vulnerability floods the group,
with no indication of misconfiguration. Reject such silent degradation at the input boundary.
Validate is used **only for writes**. Reads retain ParseFilter's tolerant semantics,
so existing invalid values do not prevent loading the entire channel.
Match decides whether an event should be delivered to a channel with this filter.
**Never returns an error**, for the same reason as ParseFilter: internal anomalies count as matches.
Evaluation order: event type -> severity threshold -> task/asset scope -> vulnerability-class keywords.
Only explicitly enabled channels receive status-change events. Disabled by default because most users
expect notifications about newly discovered vulnerabilities, not a log of every status transition.
Exclusion first: any excluded keyword rejects the event even if it also matches the include list.
Linear scans suffice for these small sets, each typically a few dozen manually selected values;
building a map costs more than it saves.
containsAnyFold reports whether s contains any keyword, case-insensitively.
This file renders email HTML bodies. Deliberately use inline styles and simple tables instead of modern CSS:
email clients (especially Outlook and domestic enterprise mail) vary greatly in their support for
<style> blocks and flex/grid; inline styles are the only consistently rendered option.
htmlSeverityColor returns the severity accent color for the left border and title.
htmlTitle returns the email subject.
htmlBody renders the email HTML body. maxRunes<=0 means no truncation.
htmlBatchIntro renders the batch email introduction: item count and severity distribution.
htmlItem renders one vulnerability. full=true includes summary and backlink (single-item delivery);
false compresses it to one line (batch list).
htmlEscape escapes HTML text. Vulnerability titles and summaries come from targets and model output,
which are untrusted; omitting escaping permits arbitrary HTML, including external images, in email.
htmlEscapeAttr escapes HTML attribute values, handling quotes in addition to text escaping
to prevent URL quotes from prematurely closing the href attribute.
allowLocalTargets controls delivery to loopback / link-local addresses.
Denied by default. IM bots and public mail servers should not use these ranges, while they can reach
sensitive destinations: management ports of colocated services and cloud metadata endpoints
(169.254.169.254, which can expose instance credentials). Administrators configure delivery URLs, but XSS/CSRF
hijacking an admin session, or another person sharing the JWT, could alter configuration to read responses:
doJSON stores the first 200 response-body bytes from 4xx/5xx responses in last_error, and delivery history
echoes it back, providing a semi-blind read primitive.
However, a local SMTP relay (postfix on 127.0.0.1:25) is common for self-hosted mail,
so a blanket ban would block legitimate users. Provide an explicit escape hatch rather than hardcoded access:
set ARTEX_NOTIFY_ALLOW_LOCAL=1 to allow it.
Export AllowLocalTargetsEnv so tests can explicitly enable this: tests in this package and server
frequently use httptest receivers on 127.0.0.1, which the guard otherwise blocks.
isBlockedDialIP reports whether a destination IP is in a range denied for delivery by default.
Reject only loopback, link-local (including cloud metadata 169.254.169.254), unspecified, and multicast addresses.
**Do not reject** RFC1918 private networks: internal Mattermost / SMTP relays are common legitimate deployments;
blocking them would make the feature unusable in real environments. This tradeoff is deliberate:
block genuinely sensitive destinations without disabling normal deployments.
Unmap IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:127.0.0.1) before checking, or it can bypass validation.
blockInternalDial is the http.Transport dialer's Control hook; it checks the destination
**when establishing the connection**.
Why enforce at dial time rather than only when saving configuration: this is the final enforcement point.
It covers two ways around configuration validation: DNS rebinding (resolving to a public IP at validation,
then an internal IP at connection time) and redirects (cross-host redirects are already denied, but same-host redirects
may still target another path).
notifyTransport adds only a dial guard to the default Transport.
Clone preserves all default tuning (connection pooling, HTTP/2, timeouts, proxy, etc.),
avoiding unrelated behavior changes just to add one check.
httpClient is shared by all channel deliveries.
Deliberately **do not** reuse the project's global outbound proxy (GlobalProxy on the server side): it carries penetration
test target traffic, often through unstable tunnels. Notification availability must not depend on target-network instability.
